text.p: He's a shade slower on his feet and will no longer make the heavyweight division after shedding 26 kg (57 pounds) due to illness, but born fighter Boris Yeltsin declared himself fully fit on Sunday and ready for a scrap.
"I have fully recovered now. I just have to gain some strength," he said after a brief wreath-laying ceremony at the Kremlin war memorial to mark Defenders of the Fatherland Day.
He said he felt his strength coming back and was more than willing to hit back at his communist and nationalist opponents in parliament who he said were spoiling for a fight.
"My brain is working fine," he told journalists eager for their first chance to quiz the 66-year-old president since he went down with pneumonia at New Year.
Yeltsin has barely seen his Kremlin office since being felled by a recurrence of heart problems at the end of a battling but too strenuous re-election campaign last July.

He had a quintuple bypass operation in November but his attempt to get back to work was cut short by the pneumonia. Doctors caution Yeltsin, still living at his Gorky-9 country home, against hurrying his return to a full schedule.

Asked about attempts by the opposition-dominated parliament to remove him on health grounds, Yeltsin showed some of his old fire, growling: "This is a purely political, communist campaign. But they should know I am a fighter and I remain a fighter. They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back."
The president, who was joined at the Eternal Flame by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other senior government figures, walked steadily if slowly and spoke clearly.
His manner seemed to bear out the assertion of U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright who found Yeltsin "very much in charge" when she met him in the Kremlin on Friday.

Albright's mission was largely devoted to continuing negotiations aimed at soothing Russia's fierce hostility to NATO's plans to extend membership of the Atlantic alliance to former Soviet-bloc countries in eastern Europe.
Yeltsin said Moscow would continue its resistance but that he expected to reach a compromise when he meets U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki next month.
"We have agreed to look for a compromise and I think we will find this compromise at the summit we are holding with President Clinton on March 20-21," he said.
Yeltsin's virtual absence from active politics since the start of his second term has been seen in the West as a hindrance to attempts to resolve the NATO dispute.
Western hopes for a quick settlement of the issue before a NATO summit in Madrid in July were raised when Yeltsin returned to the Kremlin in late December after his operation.
His latest illness may have delayed discussions but at least one Russian newspaper speculated that Yeltsin and Clinton's personal head-to-head in Helsinki could clear the air.

"Knowing that pure Yeltsin style of solving problems in one go and in the most unexpected ways, this summit could get rid of the bitterest issues dividing Moscow and Washington," the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily wrote at the weekend.
Yeltsin spent nearly 20 minutes outdoors in the bright sunshine on Sunday. Wearing a heavy dark blue coat, he ignored the freezing temperature and removed his fur hat.
The president has spoken on television and been photographed briefly during meetings with visiting officials but has not met the media or public face-to-face since New Year.
